purpose: Editorial recommendation metadata and inspected-source provenance for P23–P28, completing the voice, perspective, and dialogue family. Fields remain outside strict Commons frontmatter.

articles.title: Filter Through the Viewpoint
use_when: A scene supplies a writer's inventory rather than a particular person's encounter.
Different characters notice the same details despite different concerns.
Knowledge or interpretation enters the passage without a readable source.
mechanisms: Selecting features according to a perceiver's concerns and knowledge
Preserving enough shared spatial orientation to follow the action
not_ideal_when: The chosen narrator intentionally uses a broader or omniscient range of access.
A real person's inner experience lacks a basis in observation or an identified account.
example_user_queries: My scene describes the whole room but does not feel like anyone is seeing it.
Different viewpoint characters keep noticing the same things.
I changed the adjectives but the perspective still feels identical.
How do I choose what a character would notice right now?
My viewpoint character seems to know something they could not know.
Can a character's practical concern shape the details without naming an emotion?
I want to distinguish what someone sees from what they merely assume.
My character's profession dictates every observation and feels like a gimmick.
How much neutral description do readers need to follow the scene?
In nonfiction, can I infer what a person was thinking from their actions?

sources.author: John Larison, Oregon State University
sources.title: What is Point of View?
sources.inspected_material: The discussion of narrative perspective and third-person limited versus omniscient access, with the distinction from psychological distance.
sources.supports: Treating viewpoint as a choice about the information and perspective available to the audience.
sources.limits: No source fictional example or categorical claim about first-person heroes, second-person limits, or naturalness is adopted. The flat and visitors are original fiction; selection according to current concern is editorial development.

sources.author: Lauren Kessler
sources.title: Character: The beating heart of narrative
sources.inspected_material: Ask rather than assume, on the distinction between a nonfiction writer's projection and a subject's identified account of thought.
sources.supports: Grounding attributed inner experience in an identified source rather than plausible invention.
sources.limits: The visitors' concerns and perceptions are explicitly invented. No claim about all night workers, families, mobility needs, or the suitability of a real flat is made. Recollection and access comparisons are editorial extensions.

visual_decision.implementation: Developed prose passages show clause relationships, formal departures, and differences in perceptual selection directly. A table or graphic would add little; no interactive practice is included.

articles.title: Control Narrative Distance
use_when: An important encounter is fully explained but feels remote.
Routine events receive so much interior attention that the larger situation disappears.
Movement between overview, immediate experience, and later reflection feels unprepared.
goals: Readable movement between experience and reflection
mechanisms: Changing the relationship between narratorial explanation and immediate experience
Using an event or change of attention to motivate a movement in distance
Distinguishing the experiencing self from the later telling self
not_ideal_when: Closer narration would remove context or reflection the passage needs.
Immediate inner language would require inventing a real person's unrecorded thought.
example_user_queries: I explain how my character feels, but the important moment still seems remote.
My narration follows every hesitation and makes small events exhausting.
How can I move from an overview into a character's immediate experience?
Does first-person narration always put the reader close to the experience?
I want my older narrator to reflect without giving the younger self impossible knowledge.
When is greater narrative distance useful?
My close passage lost the context that made the scene matter.
Can I change narrative distance without changing viewpoint?
Do short sentences automatically make narration feel more intimate?
How can nonfiction convey inner experience without inventing exact thoughts?

sources.author: Emma Darwin
sources.title: Six Thoughts about Psychic Distance
sources.inspected_material: The discussion of a spectrum of distances, the value of farther positions, movement, and retrospective narration.
sources.supports: Treating closeness and overview as purposeful options, including distance between a first-person teller and an earlier experiencing self.
sources.limits: No numbered scale or source exercise is reproduced. Eleni and the departure account are original fiction. No direct review of John Gardner's book passages or universal response to closeness is claimed.

sources.author: Lauren Kessler
sources.title: Character: The beating heart of narrative
sources.inspected_material: Ask rather than assume, on grounding nonfiction thought in an identified account rather than projection.
sources.supports: Requiring a basis for attributed interior experience.
sources.limits: Exact inner phrasing, memoir uncertainty, and the distinction between remembered experience and later interpretation are editorial applications; no real inner monologue is reconstructed.

visual_decision.implementation: Developed prose passages make changes in distance, perspective, or interaction directly readable. A table or graphic would add little; no interactive practice is included.

articles.title: Make Viewpoint Shifts Legible
use_when: A private concern is attributed to the wrong person until a later name corrects the reading.
A scene changes its access to knowledge without a readable transition.
Clearly labelled viewpoints still duplicate each other's attention.
mechanisms: Anchoring the new perspective before presenting its important private knowledge
Choosing paragraph, section, or scene boundaries consistent with the established narration
Distinguishing omniscient access from changes within a limited viewpoint
not_ideal_when: The additional viewpoint contributes no useful experience or understanding.
A shift would imply access to a real person's thoughts without an identified basis.
example_user_queries: Readers keep assigning one character's thoughts to another.
How do I signal a viewpoint change before the new character's private thought?
Is a paragraph break enough to switch viewpoint?
Can I use multiple viewpoints without separate chapters?
My novel has used one limited viewpoint; how can I introduce another?
How does an omniscient narrator move between people clearly?
Does describing another character's expression count as changing viewpoint?
My character headings are clear, but the perspectives all feel the same.
Should I reveal both characters' concerns or preserve uncertainty about one?
How can reported accounts from several people stay attributable in narrative nonfiction?

sources.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
sources.title: Book View Cafe: Navigating the Ocean of Story, Session 1
sources.inspected_material: The answer to Patricia about multiple, limited, and unlimited viewpoints and the skill needed to handle changes.
sources.supports: Rejecting a blanket prohibition on multiple viewpoints while treating their handling as a craft choice.
sources.limits: The piano sale, transition boundaries, and orientation comparisons are original editorial development. No source literary example, historical generalization, or full book passage is adopted.

sources.author: Lauren Kessler
sources.title: Character: The beating heart of narrative
sources.inspected_material: Ask rather than assume, distinguishing a subject's identified account of thought from a writer's projection.
sources.supports: Preserving an evidential basis when narrative moves into real people's private experience.
sources.limits: Attribution across several accounts and differences in recollection are editorial applications. Mina, Owen, and their private concerns are original fiction.

visual_decision.implementation: Developed prose passages make changes in distance, perspective, or interaction directly readable. A table or graphic would add little; no interactive practice is included.

articles.title: Make Dialogue an Action
use_when: Speakers deliver background while the exchange remains inert.
Responses could be rearranged without affecting what happens.
Added gestures make the conversation visible but do not give its words a consequential role.
mechanisms: Connecting a speech turn to a local purpose
Letting the response alter the next attempt or available arrangement
Making information matter to the speakers' present business
not_ideal_when: A deliberately static or companionable exchange would be distorted by compulsory escalation.
A more satisfying exchange would require changing the record of real speech or inventing a speaker's motive.
example_user_queries: My dialogue gives information but the scene does not move.
Characters sound like they are reading alternating parts of a briefing.
How do I make the next line respond to what was just said?
My characters repeat the same request and refusal without developing the exchange.
Can exposition do something useful inside dialogue?
Does dialogue need conflict to have an active structure?
How can a quiet conversation about helping someone change a scene?
What is the difference between dialogue as action and dialogue with subtext?
I added gestures between speeches, but the conversation still feels inert.
How can I analyze what a real conversation does without inventing motives or changing its sequence?

sources.author: Noemi Zeigler
sources.title: Dialogue Tools and Techniques
sources.inspected_material: Writing Dialogue From Want, connecting speech to an immediate objective.
sources.supports: Examining what a speaker is trying to accomplish in the current exchange.
sources.limits: No source example or exercise is reproduced. The article does not adopt universal requirements that every line pursue a want, behaviour always precede speech, or questions never receive direct answers.

sources.author: Nicholas O’Connell
sources.title: Writing Classes for Dialogue
sources.inspected_material: The article body on scene context, interaction, resolving conflicts, reaching consensus, and action beats.
sources.supports: Treating dialogue as interaction that can develop an arrangement or consensus.
sources.limits: Both exchanges are original fiction. Cooperation, response-order comparisons, and nonfiction fidelity are editorial development. No course attendance, full book review, sidebar quotation, or compulsory conflict rule is claimed.

visual_decision.implementation: Developed prose passages make changes in distance, perspective, or interaction directly readable. A table or graphic would add little; no interactive practice is included.

articles.title: Let Dialogue Carry Subtext
use_when: Dialogue names every feeling and leaves no meaning for the reader to infer.
An intended implication depends on context the writer has not supplied.
An ordinary exchange needs to carry affection, tact, or a concern beyond its literal subject.
mechanisms: Connecting the literal subject with an established shared circumstance
Letting a response acknowledge an unspoken concern
Preserving the difference between an available inference and a definitive account of motive
not_ideal_when: Direct acknowledgment is what the people or scene need.
The intended meaning depends on an unexplained private association or an unsupported claim about a real speaker.
example_user_queries: My characters explain exactly how they feel in every conversation.
I know what is beneath the dialogue, but readers do not pick it up.
How can an ordinary conversation carry an unspoken worry?
My dialogue is so indirect that nobody knows what the speakers mean.
Can subtext show affection without hiding hostility?
How much context does a reader need to interpret a practical question?
I keep adding a sentence after dialogue to explain its emotional meaning.
Can a character finally say the thing openly without ruining the scene?
Does every reply have to dodge the question to make dialogue interesting?
How do I distinguish an interpretation of real speech from a reported motive?

sources.author: Noemi Zeigler
sources.title: Dialogue Tools and Techniques
sources.inspected_material: Subtext (What’s Not Said), distinguishing spoken content from underlying meaning.
sources.supports: Treating an exchange as capable of carrying meaning that is not stated explicitly.
sources.limits: No source dialogue or exercise is reproduced. The article does not adopt the generalization that people rarely say what they mean, or a requirement to evade questions. Ruth, Nell, and their Tuesday meal are original fiction.

sources.author: Suzzanna Matthews, UCD Writing Centre
sources.title: Revising and Editing Fiction
sources.inspected_material: Revising Dialogue, Subtext and Context, on pages 2–3 of the six-page handout.
sources.supports: Reading words together with context and staging rather than adding a redundant account of tone.
sources.limits: Only this dialogue guidance is used. No source example, generalization about body language, or unrelated advice on narrative structure, point of view, or passive voice is adopted. Limits of inference, direct acknowledgment, and nonfiction applications are editorial development.

visual_decision.implementation: Self-contained prose examples make implication, speaker ownership, or local intention directly readable. A table or graphic would add little; no interactive practice is included.

articles.title: Keep Speech Attribution Clear and Light
use_when: Readers have to count turns or revise an earlier guess about who spoke.
A third speaker or long interruption breaks the established alternation.
Decorative tags and repeated gestures compete with the exchange.
mechanisms: Placing identification before speaker ownership changes interpretation
Using simple tags and omitting them where the surrounding exchange provides enough orientation
Choosing action beats and manner details for information beyond avoiding repeated said
not_ideal_when: Omitting attribution would obscure the source of an important line or real quotation.
An unusual speech verb, delivery detail, or explicit repeated name communicates necessary information.
example_user_queries: Readers keep losing track of who is speaking.
I removed dialogue tags and now the conversation is hard to follow.
How should I handle attribution when a third person joins the conversation?
The speaker is named only at the end of a long speech and readers have to reread it.
I keep replacing said with fancy verbs and the dialogue feels overdone.
Do I need a gesture between every pair of dialogue lines?
When is it useful to repeat a character’s name instead of a pronoun?
Can whispering or another delivery detail matter even when the words are clear?
How can I keep a quick exchange clear without slowing it down?
How much attribution can I remove from nonfiction quotations without obscuring their sources?

sources.author: Suzzanna Matthews, UCD Writing Centre
sources.title: Revising and Editing Fiction
sources.inspected_material: The dialogue-tag and staging guidance on pages 2–3.
sources.supports: Using simple identifying tags and meaningful staging rather than distracting attribution.
sources.limits: No fixed ratio of said to other tags, automatic interpretation of gestures, source example, or unrelated point-of-view rule is adopted. The radio and theatre scenes are original fiction.

sources.title: Is it necessary to indicate who is speaking for every line of dialogue?
sources.inspected_material: The explanation of tags, paragraphing, action, and exchanges whose speakers remain clear without tagging every line.
sources.supports: Combining forms of orientation according to the passage rather than attributing every turn.
sources.limits: The source’s Egan extract is not reproduced or treated as a review of the full story. Three-speaker orientation, early placement, sound reach, and nonfiction applications are original editorial development. No direct inspection of Stephen King’s book passages is claimed.
